title: Paying Down High-Interest Debt
summary: Settle urgent accounts, keep required payments on track and aim every safe extra dollar at one target.
subtitle: Your Debt List Has Too Many Guests. The 29.99% Balance Has Been Eating All the Snacks.

blocks.text: High-interest debt sends more of every payment to interest and leaves less to pay down the balance.
Throwing money at every balance at random won’t work. Settle urgent accounts, keep required payments on track, stop new borrowing and send extra money to one target you have checked.

In this High-Interest Debt Triage Room, you will build a Debt Emergency Inventory and sort each balance by danger, damage and drain. The aim is a plan that works on an ordinary payday, not a heroic one that survives until about Wednesday.
FCAC: Paying back your debt
The highest interest rate usually deserves the extra payment. An urgent housing, utility, secured-payment or legal problem may still need fixing first.

blocks.text: The Three-Part Triage Map

items.title: LAYER 1 — DANGER
items.text: Spot past-due essentials, secured debts, collection or legal notices, and any account about to lose service, be repossessed or face another serious result. Check the deadline and call the creditor soon.

items.title: LAYER 2 — DAMAGE
items.text: Keep paying the required minimum or agreed amount on every account you can. A missed payment can bring fees, higher rates, collection calls or damage to your credit report.

items.title: LAYER 3 — DRAIN
items.text: Once urgent accounts and required payments are covered, send extra money to the high-interest target you have checked. Stop adding new purchases to it while you pay it down.

items.title: “The fairest plan is to split every extra dollar equally among all debts.”
items.text: Equal isn’t always efficient. Once urgent accounts and required payments are covered, putting extra money on one high-interest target usually cuts interest faster than spreading it thin.

blocks.text: One verified target beats five scattered payments, and the inventory ahead finds it in minutes.
blocks.detail: Sorting your debts by real urgency, not by which one feels loudest, is how the extra dollars stop disappearing.
blocks.extra: Five real balances get sorted by danger, damage and drain next.

sections.title: Debt Emergency Inventory: See the Whole Waiting Room

blocks.text: The figures below are made up. Tara copies from current statements and notices, not from remembered balances, advertised rates or numbers that have been living comfortably in her imagination.

items.title: PAST-DUE UTILITY
items.text: $240 — Service-risk notice — What is the deadline, the smallest plan they will accept and the confirmation number?

items.title: STORE CARD
items.text: $1,050 at 29.99% — Minimum: $35 — Highest rate; are new purchases and optional add-ons stopped?

items.title: CREDIT CARD
items.text: $2,800 at 22.99% — Minimum: $84 — Is the rate current, and does a penalty rate kick in after missed payments?

items.title: LINE OF CREDIT
items.text: $3,600 at 11.50% — Minimum: $75 — Is the rate variable, and what makes it change?

items.title: CAR LOAN
items.text: $7,900 at 7.49% — Payment: $310 — Is the account current, secured and essential for work?

blocks.text: Triage Order Is Not Simply Balance Order

items.title: FIRST
items.text: Tara calls the utility before the notice deadline and gets a written two-payment plan: $120 this month and $120 next month.

items.title: SECOND
items.text: She keeps every required debt payment on track and checks the due dates. If the budget can’t cover them, she calls creditors before the due date instead of waiting for a missed-payment alert.

items.title: THIRD
items.text: For two months, $105 of her $225 extra goes to the 29.99% store card after the $120 utility payment. In month three, the full $225 goes to the store card.

items.title: “The biggest balance must be the most expensive debt.”
items.text: Balance affects how many dollars of interest you pay, but the rate shows how hard each dollar is priced. Look at balance, rate, status and consequence together. Size alone doesn’t set the order.

blocks.text: A smaller balance with a high rate can be a great first target. It is expensive, and it may be gone sooner once urgent accounts are settled.
Meet Tara
paragraphs: Tara lives in Edmonton. She has five debts, one past-due utility notice and $225 a month left after essentials and required payments. The store card is waving a 29.99% rate like it has diplomatic immunity.
Then the utility’s final notice arrives: pay $240 before the deadline or lose power. Every balance wants to be called first.

Tara lays the five statements across the table. The $7,900 car loan is the biggest balance. The credit card makes the most interest each month, while the store card charges the highest rate. All three feel urgent.

Her first instinct is to throw the $225 at the car loan, because it dominates the page. Then she stops. It is current, secured and low-rate, so it is not the emergency. A cash advance would make the whole plan look complete, but that is new high-cost borrowing to stage a photograph of progress. She drops that idea too and calls the utility and the card issuers.

The math adds a twist. The credit card costs about $53.64 a month in interest. The store card costs about $26.24. The bigger bill has the lower rate. Each dollar on the store card saves more than a dollar on the credit card. After she protects the utility plan and every required payment, she picks the store card as her target.

Over 90 days, Tara makes every required payment, finishes the $240 utility plan and sends $435 of planned extra money to the store card. She makes no new purchases on it and keeps every written confirmation. No new debt has slipped in wearing a fake moustache. The store card’s diplomatic immunity has been revoked.

blocks.text: Tara's triage order kept her lights on and still knocked out her worst-rate card.
blocks.detail: The five-step response that got Tara through her waiting room works the same way on your own five balances.
blocks.extra: Section 03 lays out the same five-step response, in order.

items.title: LAYER 1 — VERIFY
items.text: Write down the creditor, balance, yearly rate or APR, minimum, due date, status, whether it is secured, and any notice or special penalty. Mark what you don’t know for a call to the creditor.

items.title: LAYER 2 — STABILIZE
items.text: Protect housing, utilities and other essentials. Deal with past-due and secured accounts. Get payment plans in writing when you can.

items.title: LAYER 3 — HOLD THE LINE
items.text: Make the required payments you can afford, pause new charges, remove saved card details and stop optional repeat charges from hitting the target account.

items.title: LAYER 4 — TARGET
items.text: Send every planned extra dollar to one high-interest balance. Make it automatic or tied to payday when you can, but keep enough cash for essentials.

items.title: LAYER 5 — ROLL FORWARD
items.text: When the target is paid off, move its old required payment plus the extra amount to the next target. Check rates and account status each month.

blocks.text: A quick training estimate is balance × annual rate ÷ 12.
Statements may work out interest daily, use average daily balances, compound differently, or include purchases and fees. Use your statement for the real charge.

items.text: $1,050 × 29.99% ÷ 12 ≈ $26.24 — An estimate for one month, before new activity and payment timing.

items.title: CREDIT CARD
items.text: $2,800 × 22.99% ÷ 12 ≈ $53.64 — Its lower rate still costs more dollars because the balance is bigger.

items.title: LINE OF CREDIT
items.text: $3,600 × 11.50% ÷ 12 = $34.50 — Check the current variable rate before you trust the estimate.

items.title: “Making the minimum payment means the debt is being handled efficiently.”
items.text: A minimum keeps an account current, but it may pay down the balance slowly and stretch out the interest. Pay more than the minimum when you safely can, and keep your other required payments current.

blocks.text: A payment is not the same as paying down the balance. Interest and fees may take their share first. The statement shows what reached the balance.

sections.title: Reduce the Rate Without Rebuilding the Debt

items.title: Ask the current creditor.
items.text: Ask for a lower-rate product, a hardship option or a payment plan. Get the rate, fees, term, effect on the account and total cost in writing.

items.title: Compare consolidation carefully.
items.text: A lower rate may save money, but a longer term, fees or new borrowing can raise the total cost. Compare the same balances and the same payoff date.

items.title: Protect collateral.
items.text: Moving unsecured debt onto a secured product may put your home or another asset at risk. A lower rate is not free protection.

items.title: Close the refill path.
items.text: If consolidation pays off a card, decide how you will control the empty account. That way you don’t end up with the new loan plus a rebuilt card balance.

items.title: “Consolidation always saves money because one payment is simpler.”
items.text: One payment may be easier to manage, but real savings need a lower total cost, not just a lower monthly payment. Check the rate, fees, term, total repayment, collateral and whether old balances can come back.

blocks.text: A lower payment from a longer term can feel like relief while quietly buying you more years of interest. Compare the payoff date as carefully as the payment.
FCAC: Debt consolidation
When the Numbers Need More Than a Worksheet

Get qualified help early if required payments don’t fit after essentials, accounts stay past due, collection or legal action is under way, or new borrowing is paying old debts. Credit counsellors can talk through debt management plans, but creditors choose whether to accept them, and fees matter. Only Licensed Insolvency Trustees can run consumer proposals and bankruptcies.
Province Lens: Collection Rules Are Local

Collection rules differ in Alberta, British Columbia, New Brunswick, Ontario, Prince Edward Island, and Newfoundland and Labrador. Check who the collector is, what the debt is and how much is owed. Keep records and use your province’s current authority. Consumer proposals and bankruptcies are federal processes run by Licensed Insolvency Trustees.

items.title: Past-due essential with a service-risk date.
items.detail: Call and settle it before the deadline.

items.title: All accounts current; extra money available.
items.detail: Keep up the minimums, then target the highest rate you have checked.

items.title: Lower consolidation payment over twice as long.
items.detail: Compare fees, total cost and payoff date.

items.title: Minimums no longer fit.
items.detail: Call creditors and get qualified help before you miss more payments.

items.title: Target card cleared.
items.detail: Roll its old payment into the next target.

blocks.text: Before You Build Your Own Debt Emergency Inventory

items.title: “Asking for debt help means I have failed, and every debt-relief company offers the same protection.”
items.text: Getting help early is a smart way to control risk. Providers have different roles and authority. Check credentials, services, fees and promises, and avoid anyone who guarantees a quick credit-score fix or asks for money for a result they can’t legally deliver.

blocks.text: A debt-management plan is not the same as a consumer proposal or bankruptcy. Ask who regulates the provider, which creditors have to agree and what happens to debts outside the plan.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Debt Emergency Inventory

blocks.text: Use shortened creditor names.
Do not record full account numbers, passwords, card details, PINs, security answers or government ID numbers in course notes.
High-Interest Debt Triage Closing Checklist

items.title: Every debt is verified.
items.text: Balance, rate, required payment, due date, status, security and notices come from current records.

items.title: Immediate danger is under control.
items.text: Risks to essential services, secured debts, collections and legal matters each have a dated contact or a written plan.

items.title: The payment floor is protected.
items.text: Required payments are scheduled, and any shortfall means a call before the due date.

items.title: One target receives the extra.
items.text: The amount and payday transfer are specific, and new charges are blocked.

items.title: The plan has an escalation line.
items.text: Repeated shortfalls, collection activity or borrowing to pay bills means getting qualified help.

blocks.text: Settle urgent problems and protect required payments first.
blocks.detail: Stop new charges, put safe extra money on one target and get qualified help before the plan stops working.

blocks.text: Don’t judge debt progress by how dramatic the plan sounds. Judge it by fewer urgent accounts, no missed required payments, a falling target balance and no new high-interest borrowing.
SOURCE REVIEW DATE: 11 August 2026. Recheck rates, rules, provider credentials and provincial contacts before you rely on this lesson.

items.title: High-interest debt
items.text: Debt with a rate so high that it costs a lot to carry and slows how fast you pay down what you owe.

items.title: Principal
items.text: The amount you owe, before future interest and fees.

items.title: Minimum payment
items.text: The smallest payment the creditor requires each period. It is not meant to pay the debt off fast.

items.title: Past due
items.text: A required payment that did not arrive by its due date.

items.title: Secured debt
items.text: Debt backed by something you own, which you could lose if you break the agreement.

items.title: Unsecured debt
items.text: Debt that isn’t backed by a specific asset, such as many credit cards and personal loans.

items.title: Target debt
items.text: The one balance that gets the planned extra payments once urgent items and required payments are covered.

items.title: Debt consolidation
items.text: Rolling several debts into one loan or product, ideally at a lower total cost and a term you can handle.

items.title: Debt management plan
items.text: An informal repayment plan set up through a credit counsellor. Creditors choose whether to take part.

items.title: Licensed Insolvency Trustee
items.text: A federally regulated professional who is allowed to run consumer proposals and bankruptcies in Canada.

quiz.question: True or False: “The fairest plan is to split every extra dollar equally among all debts.”

questions: List each debt you owe: creditor, balance, rate, required payment and due date. An estimate is fine.
Which debt has the most urgent problem, such as a past-due bill, a collection notice or a secured item? Write the deadline and who to call.
What do your required payments add up to each month? Do they fit after housing, food, utilities and transport?
For one credit card, estimate a month of interest: balance × rate ÷ 12. How does it compare with your statement?
After urgent items and required payments, which debt gets your extra money, and why?
What is your 30-day plan? Write the extra payment, the date you will send it and where the money comes from. Who will you call for help if you fall behind?
